courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Media and Social Development in Mainland China
courses.description:
(UGEC2634 is double-coded with COMM2140.)

The course is designed around two major themes, namely media and social development in Mainland China since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. Using key concepts and theories from the political economy of media and developmental communication studies, it introduces students to different periods of media reform and social change from the era of Chairman Mao to the period of "harmonious society". Emphasis is attached to post-1989 media regulatory systems, media industrialization, and their influence on the meeting of such developmental goals as poverty alleviation, democratization, and communication empowerment.

The course will examine Mainland China's key media sectors including the printing press (newspapers and magazines), film and broadcasting media (radio and TV), and new networked communication tools (Internet and mobile phone) as well as alternative social formations through Internet activism, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and transnational developmental projects. The course will identify and discuss several ongoing debates, and the ensuing actions, held by different stakeholders, including governmental officials, media producers, educators, activists, international agencies, and the general audiences. Wider implications to public policy will be identified. There will also be discussions of current affairs related to media and social development in the country.

Students will be able to describe the key characteristics of contemporary Mainland Chinese media and their roles in facilitating or obstructing development towards the ideals of a "new China".
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will be able to describe key characteristics of media in Mainland China.

2. Students will be able to discuss how media influences social development and how new social formations trigger media reform in Mainland China.

3. Students will be able to identify phases of media and social development in Mainland China and differentiate policymaking rationales in different media sectors (printing, broadcasting, networked media) and types of social movements.

4. Students will be able to discuss competing arguments about the role of media reform in China's modernization drive.

5. Students will be able to produce a media text that offers a critique to one of the historical periods, media industries, or controversial issues covered in the course.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course consists of five main parts: (I) theories of media, communication and social development (week 1 and 2); (II) history of media transformation in Mainland China since 1949 (week 3 and 4); (III) key media sectors (week 5 to 7); (IV) social movements and campaigns (week 8 to 10); and (V) institutional stakeholders (week 11 and 12). In each part, there will be a mixture of conceptual and practical information, of consensus and controversies, and of historical knowledge and current affairs. The class will also look at different disadvantaged social groups and their relationship with various media sectors and stakeholders both within and outside officialdom.

The following is an outline of the course:

* *Week 1 Introduction: Ideals of "New China"**

The first class will introduce students to (a) the pursuit of a "New China" that gave legitimacy to the rise of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) since the May Fourth Movement, and (b) classical theories of media and national development between 1950s and 1980s. It will also discuss the concept of 'social development' and give an overview of the course's core content.

* Key concepts: "New China", nation building, communication and development*

* *Week 2 Communist Media Theories: Political Control and Social Development**

This class discusses Leninist press theory, its evolution in the Chinese party-state, and the rationale behind this historical transformation, including politico-economic considerations as well as trends in cultural and technological change. Key ideas of the mass line and ICTD (information and communication technologies and development) will also be discussed in the case of rural development.

* Key concepts: Leninist press theory, party-state, political control, the mass line, ICTD, rural development*

* *Week 3 and 4 Past and Present**

These two classes differentiate media and social development in Mainland China into three historical periods: 1949-1978; 1978-1989; and 1989-date. What defines these periods? How are they different? Did previous periods pave the way for later trends of marketization and partial liberalization in the post-1989 era?

* Key concepts: The Maoist era, pre-1989 media reform, post-1989 reform, marketization, partial liberalization*

* *Weeks 5 to 7 Key Media Sectors**

Zooming into China's printing media (newspaper and magazines), film and broadcasting media (radio and TV), and new networked media (Internet and mobile phone), these three classes provide a sector-specific analysis of China's media systems and their contributions to meeting goals of social development. Issues of censorship and regulation will be introduced. Debates on the digital divide will also be discussed.

* Key concepts: printing media, film, broadcasting media, networked media, censorship, regulation, digital divide*

* *Weeks 8 to 10 Social Movements and Campaigns**

These three classes focus on official efforts to modernize China using traditional and new media channels as well as alternative communication empowerment projects such as those led by domestic labor NGOs, environmental groups, and transnational civil society players. Studies in minority-nationality regions and with regard to disadvantaged groups such as women will be discussed along with the official project of "constructing new socialist countryside".

* Key concepts: "constructing new socialist countryside", activism, empowerment, feminist activism, environmental movement, minority nationalities, transnational civil society*

* *Week 11 and 12 Institutional Stakeholders**

We will first return to China's media regulatory frameworks centered on the CCP's Central Propaganda Division (CPD) as well as several ministry-level governing bodies whose bureaucratic systems extend to lower levels of the party-state. Then in Week 12, we will look into China's journalism education system as another key institutional stakeholder. To what extent are the regulators and educators facilitating or hindering overall social development? Why? How could they do better? How could college students in Hong Kong play a meaningful role interacting with the stakeholders?

* Key concepts: CPD, local state, media governance, journalism education, democratization*

* *Week 13 Student Group Presentations and Course Wrap-Up**

Students will present their final projects in the last class, which will end with the instructor's wrap-up of the course.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: Media Research: Psychological and Sociological Perspectives
courses.description: This course offers a comprehensive introduction to media research from psychological and sociological perspectives. Students will examine a wide range of topics, including media effects, media organizations, media events, audience behavior, and the political economy of media. The course is designed to help students understand the reciprocal relationship between media, individual psychology, and social structures, while fostering an interdisciplinary analytical approach.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Describe and apply key psychological and sociological theories to analyze media phenomena, including media effects and audience behavior.
2. Critically examine media institutions and organizations, exploring their roles in shaping content, public discourse, and societal values.
3. Analyze media events as socially constructed phenomena, considering their psychological impact and sociological significance.
4. Evaluate the political economy of media, including ownership structures, regulatory frameworks, and the influence of economic forces on media production and distribution.
5. Interpret audience responses to media content using psychological models and sociological frameworks.
6. Assess the reciprocal relationship between media, individual psychology, and social structures, identifying patterns of influence and feedback.

courses.subject: COMM
courses.title: News Analysis
courses.description:
(UGEC2621 is double-coded with COMM2910.)

Theories and methods in news sociology in understanding the news-making process and its impacts on the product itself and the society. Students also learn to conduct their own analysis of news in local or foreign media.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken COMM2210/UGEC2623 or UGEC2621.
courses.learning_outcomes:
The aim of this course is three-fold. First, it is designed to introduce students to various conceptual approaches to news. Second, the "media logic" of each news medium will be analysed. Third, students shall zero in on some key aspects of news and use conceptual tools to analyse various news phenomena. Emphasis will be on the local news media.

This course is intended to sharpen students' conceptual framework and generic attribute of analytical thinking.
courses.course_syllabus: This course deals with some conceptual issues such as the nature and significance of news, frameworks of news analysis, models of news production, market-driven journalism, and the social roles of news. It will also focus on the "grammar" of each news medium, including newspaper, radio, television, and news website. The news format, layout, strengths and weaknesses of each medium will be examined. In addition, various factors affecting news agendas, news sources and news angles, news benefactors and victims, international news reporting, as well as some news trends in recent years will be studied.

4. Apply qualitative research methods such as interviews, textual analysis, and ethnography in communication studies.
5. Design and conduct independent qualitative research projects in media and communication.
6. Demonstrate academic writing skills appropriate for qualitative research in communication.

courses.title: Health and Environmental Journalism
courses.description:
This course offers students a foundational understanding of health and environmental journalism as specialized areas within the field of journalism. It introduces pressing global and local issues, such as public health crises, climate change, pollution, and food safety, that have profound impacts on society and are increasingly featured in news coverage.
Students will examine the historical development and current trends of these topics, explore the roles of key stakeholders including governments, NGOs, scientists, and affected communities, and develop the analytical and storytelling skills essential for reporting on complex health and environmental matters. By placing journalistic practices within wider social, ethical, and political contexts, the course aims to nurture responsible and informed journalists who can effectively engage the public and promote awareness and positive change.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completing the course, students will be able to:

* Identify key stakeholders in health and environmental journalism and describe their respective interests and roles.
* List major health and environmental issues and outline their current status and emerging trends.
* Combine basic reporting techniques with domain-specific knowledge to produce informative content.
* Follow standard procedures for verifying sources and conducting interviews.

* Analyse the interplay between stakeholders and its influence on media narratives and public understanding.
* Apply ethical principles and storytelling techniques to present complex health and environmental information clearly and persuasively.
* Compare and contrast reliable information with misinformation, disinformation, and propaganda in health and environmental reporting.
* Relate journalistic practices to broader social, cultural, and political contexts.

* Reflect critically on the role of journalism in shaping public discourse, health awareness, and environmental policy.
* Generalize principles of ethical journalism to diverse reporting contexts and hypothesize the implications of emerging health and environmental trends for future media practices.
* Theorize how journalism can contribute to sustainable development and public well-being through responsible reporting.

(For Reference Only. Subject to Change)

* Introduction to health journalism and the healthcare system
* Medical knowledge, integrity, and conflicts of interest
* Medical regulation and ethical considerations
* Healthcare policies
* Innovative and investigative approaches to health reporting
* Simulated press conference

Environmental Journalism

* Introduction to environmental journalism and the role of environmental journalists
* The role of environmental organizations in agenda-setting
* Field trip
* Global trends in environmental issues
* Corporate environmentalism — genuine commitment or greenwashing?
* Environmental news topics in conservation and urban planning

courses.description: This course explores the critical role of strategic communication in entrepreneurial success. It equips students with the skills to craft compelling messages, build stakeholder relationships, and manage brand reputation in dynamic business environments. Students will learn how to communicate effectively with investors, customers, partners, and the media, while aligning communication strategies with business goals. * Evaluate the impact of communication efforts using appropriate metrics and feedback mechanisms to refine strategies and improve outcomes.
* Demonstrate readiness for entrepreneurial ventures or communication roles in start-ups, with the ability to manage strategic messaging and stakeholder communication.

courses.title: Social Responsibility and Sustainability Communication
courses.description:
This course seeks to provide the knowledge and skills needed to research, plan, and implement communication campaigns for corporate social responsibility (CSR) and sustainability practices. The course examines theories and practices related to CSR in order to understand the business environment in which public relations/advertising operate and apply them to developing and evaluating communication campaigns.
Specifically, this course provides an overview of CSR, its evolution, and theories in management and psychology that underlay strategic approaches and consumer behavior. It also covers the planning and integration of media into strategic CSR communication programmes. Students will learn to set objectives, develop CSR campaign plans, integrate traditional and social media into overall communication plans, measure program results, utilize new media technologies, and about the macro-environmental issues affecting CSR governance.

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

1. Understand the concepts and principles of corporate social responsibility (CSR) and sustainability.
2. Analyze how different stakeholders expect, influence, and engage with organizations’ CSR and sustainability practices.
3. Understand various models and types of CSR practices and their outcomes.
4. Understand roles and challenges in CSR and sustainability communications.
5. Explain how strategic communication planning is integrated into CSR and sustainability practices.
6. Develop a strategic communication plan for CSR and sustainability initiatives.

courses.description: This course introduces common multivariate techniques, logics, methods and their applications in communication and social sciences. Students are expected to understand various assumptions of and rationalities behind various statistical methods, learn the techniques and uses, and apply them to their own research. The course aims at strengthening students' ability in formulating research questions, validating theories and applying appropriate methodologies, regardless of what research directions (quantitative of qualitative) they are interested in.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil Communication or PhD Communication
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of the course, students should gain a clear understanding of the concepts and techniques of multivariate data analysis. Students should be able to:
• Determine which multivariate technique is appropriate for a specific research problem;
• Use SPSS to perform various multivariate statistical analyses; and
• Perform and interpret various multivariate statistical tests including scale construction, factor analysis, multiple regression, MANOVA, discriminant analysis, logistic regression, path analysis and structural equation modeling.
